title: Heaven's wide net
hookLine: heaven's net is wide and loose, yet nothing slips through (Tao Te Ching 73)

cards: A fishing net hangs drying on a fence. The holes are big enough to put a fist through, and water runs straight through it. It looks like it couldn't hold anything.

And yet, cast the right way, at the right depth, it comes back full. Chapter seventy-three of the Tao Te Ching hangs a net like that over the whole world. Before it gets there, it talks about two kinds of courage.

teach.b: First, the two kinds of courage. Bold in daring, and you're killed; bold in not daring, and you live. One brings benefit, one brings harm.
Then the chapter shrugs: what heaven dislikes, who knows the reason? Even the sage finds this hard. That honesty matters; the chapter doesn't pretend the world's workings are easy to read.
It doesn't fight, yet it's good at winning. It doesn't speak, yet it's good at answering. It isn't summoned, yet it comes on its own.
It seems slack, unhurried, yet it plans well. Every line pairs an absence with a result. Third, the net.
Heaven's net is vast, its mesh is wide, and yet nothing is lost. It isn't tight; it doesn't grab or chase. Still nothing falls out of it.
Readers take this a few ways: as a promise that things come back around, as reassurance that the world holds together without anyone clutching, or as a warning that nothing done is really hidden.

Fourth, loosening the grip. A lot of worry is an attempt to tighten the mesh: to check every thread, control every outcome, close every gap yourself. Heaven's net is a different picture: loose, patient, and holding.
Not every result will be the one you want. But the clutching isn't what holds it.

how: Readers of the Tao Te Ching often take chapter seventy-three's wide-meshed net as a picture of a world that holds together without force, and some read it as a reminder that nothing done stays hidden.

o: a wide-meshed net that still loses nothing
a fisherman's prayer for a good day's catch
the stars, seen as a net across the night sky

s: chapter seventy-three says heaven's net is fine and tight
it says the net is vast and wide-meshed, and yet nothing is lost.
the chapter admits even the sage finds heaven's reasons hard
what heaven dislikes, it asks, who knows why? even the sage finds it hard.
the chapter says heaven's way comes without being summoned
it isn't called, yet it comes on its own.

games.q: you're facing a risk. chapter seventy-three names two kinds of courage. which one does it say leads to life?
games.why: bold in daring, and you're killed; bold in not daring, and you live. then the chapter admits nobody fully knows heaven's reasons.

practice: Let the breath come and go without managing it, and bring to mind one thing you've been gripping: a result you're waiting on, a situation you keep checking. Picture it resting in a wide net, holes and all; you've done your part.
When the urge to check or fix comes back, let the mesh stay loose.

wordCard.voice: Heaven's net. Chapter seventy-three: vast, wide-meshed, and yet nothing slips through. Today's word.

orig.note: Chinese: heaven's net is vast, from chapter seventy-three.

carryVoice: Your line: heaven's way holds without grabbing. Wide mesh, and nothing lost. Go gently today, and I'll see you tomorrow.

sources.ref: Tao Te Ching 73 (courage in daring and in not daring; who knows what heaven dislikes; heaven's way does not contend yet wins; heaven's net is vast and wide-meshed yet loses nothing)
